items.title: [popsci.com] Nearby giant likely tilted hot Jupiter out of view
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b, about 1,000 light-years away, stopped transiting its star in March 2026 because the gravitational pull of a nearby, still-unseen planet tilted its orbit out of Earth’s line of sight. NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed the system from April 2019 to March 2026; the planet circles its star every 8.25 days. Before the transits vanished, they arrived as much as six hours early or late and grew shorter and shallower, signs that the orbit’s alignment was changing. How the planet moved close to its star remains uncertain. The study appeared in *The Astrophysical Journal Letters* on Nov. 9. TOI-2535 b is not expected to transit again for at least 30 years, while its companion could become visible in transit sooner.

items.title: [space.com] Apollo 12 lightning strikes prompted NASA to tighten launch weather rules
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Johns Hopkins scientists have uncovered hidden warning signs of Alzheimer’s disease that may appear up to a decade before memory loss begins. Brain scans revealed that two regions involved in memory and emotion start shrinking before the hippocampus, the area doctors typically examine for signs of Alzheimer’s. These early changes are linked to abnormal tau protein buildup and could provide a powerful new way to identify people at risk.

items.title: [meatingplace.com] H5N1 detections hit 40 Washington dairy herds as cases surge
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Bird flu spread quickly through Central Washington dairy farms in October, with 40 Washington herds testing positive from Oct. 7 to Oct. 30, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture; 33 were in Yakima County and one was in neighboring Benton County. Officials confirmed the first two cases at Yakima County dairies on Oct. 8 and four additional cases on Oct. 29. A Yakima County resident exposed to infected dairy cattle died Nov. 1, and local officials also reported two other human infections linked to cattle. Containing the virus is difficult because cattle farms cannot be sealed and controlled as tightly as poultry barns, said Rick Naerbout, executive director of the Washington State Dairy Federation. The federation advised farmers on Oct. 4 to follow biosecurity plans and alert veterinarians to falling milk production; researchers have not established the virus’s natural route of spread among cows. Washington officials say infected cows generally recover within four to six weeks, and state agriculture officials say pasteurized milk remains safe.

items.title: [dagenslantbruk.se] Farmers urged to tailor grazing to grassland recovery and climate
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Agricultural specialists in Sweden, France and South Africa say grassland management requires continued upkeep and grazing adapted to local vegetation and weather. Sweden’s inventory found that the natural and cultural values of most re-surveyed meadows and pastures remained broadly stable, while French livestock farmers discussed how the 2026 drought and heat affected forage production. University of Limpopo pasture scientist Lesego Motshekga says rotational grazing works only when stocking rates match available forage and plants have time to recover; moving animals between camps alone cannot prevent overgrazing. Motshekga recommends deciding when to move livestock based on grass condition rather than a fixed calendar.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Security teams in Jaramana searched vehicles and checked surveillance cameras after a car bomb struck a residential area near al-Naseem garage, damaging nearby cars and buildings, according to reports. The blast on Saturday, Nov. 14, killed a man and a girl, according to medical sources cited by Asharq Al-Awsat and Al Jazeera. Reports differed on the number of wounded: Syria’s state television said two people were wounded, while the Interior Ministry reported one. The explosion occurred near a battery-production site in Jaramana, a Damascus suburb with a large Druze community. Syria’s Internal Security Forces cordoned off the area and opened an investigation. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said accounts differed over the blast’s precise location and nature, and verification was continuing. Residents told Asharq Al-Awsat they heard the blast at about 8 p.m. and saw the car burning. Security vehicles arrived within minutes, and streets leading to the site were closed, with access allowed for ambulances and civil defense crews.
